title: Gregory of Narek (27 February)
hook: an Armenian monk whose Book of Lamentations is a conversation with God from the depths

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter Damian, the monk who wrote hard letters to popes and signed himself a sinner. Your line was blunt love.

In some Armenian homes there's a book kept near the bed, or tucked under the pillow of someone who is sick. It's a book of prayers, and people often call it simply by its author's village: the Narek. Tradition says families read from it at bedsides and in hard nights, the way others keep a rosary in a pocket. Its author was a monk at a monastery called Narek, by a lake in Armenia, long ago. His book starts from the bottom.
screen: `A BOOK UNDER THE PILLOW.` → `THEY CALL IT THE NAREK.` → `A MONK BY A LAKE.`

segments.voice: Gregory called his book a Book of Lamentations. Each of its prayers, by tradition, opens with the same phrase, which can be put in English as speaking with God from the depths of the heart. Gregory doesn't write as a holy man explaining prayer to beginners. He writes as someone who has looked honestly at himself and doesn't like all he sees. He piles up images for his own brokenness: a ship breaking apart, a field gone to weeds, a debtor with nothing to pay. Page after page, he refuses to pretend. And then, again and again, he turns: not to his own goodness, which he's just given up on, but to God's mercy, which he trusts more than his own despair. He even prays for the people who will read him, and for those who wrong him. That shape is old; the Psalms have it. In the Douay-Rheims, the psalm Catholics know as the De profundis begins: "Out of the depths I have cried to thee, O Lord: Lord, hear my voice." Gregory's book reads like that first line, carried across page after page. He belongs first to the Armenian Apostolic Church, which honors him as a saint. Armenian Catholics honor him too, and Pope Francis named him a Doctor of the Church, a teacher for the whole Catholic Church. A monk who wrote so honestly about how lost he was became a teacher. Prayer doesn't have to start from the top.
screen: `SPEAKING WITH GOD FROM THE DEPTHS.` · `HONEST ABOUT HIS OWN BROKENNESS.` · `THEN TURNING TO MERCY.` · `AN ARMENIAN DOCTOR OF THE CHURCH.` · then, large: `OUT OF THE DEPTHS I HAVE CRIED TO THEE.`

segments.voice: Let one honest thing rise, something you're carrying that isn't tidy, a failure, a fear, a grudge, a tiredness, and don't dress it up or argue it down. Then turn, the way Gregory does: if you pray, say the psalm's first line, out of the depths I have cried to thee, O Lord, and leave the rest to God. If you don't, breathe out slowly and let the heavy thing sit beside you rather than on top of you.
De profundis, Latin for out of the depths, the psalm Gregory of Narek's prayers echo. An Armenian monk, he speaks with God from the depths of the heart, and is a Doctor of the Church.
Your line: the book of lamentations. Honest about the bottom, and turned toward mercy. That's day nine hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Armenian Christians, both Apostolic and Catholic, honor Saint Gregory of Narek, and some families keep his Book of Lamentations at home for prayer, especially in illness; in the Roman calendar he is remembered on 27 February.
